## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

Table 1 ranks the enriched biological pathways on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and relevance to stroke pathophysiology. Immune-related and inflammatory pathways are prominently represented across multiple annotation sources. These include antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via major histocompatibility complex class one (Gene Ontology:0002474, p = 3.38 × 10−3), Interleukin ten signaling (Reactome:R-HSA-6783783, p = 9.39 × 10−5), cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, p = 5.32 × 10−16), tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (Reactome:R-HSA-5669034, p = 5.55 × 10−10), and regulation of leukocyte activation (Gene Ontology:0002694, p = 1.03 × 10−8). Collectively, these terms span p-values from 3.38 × 10−3 to 5.32 × 10−16, indicating strong statistical support for immune system involvement. This pattern is consistent with prior evidence that stroke is accompanied by rapid activation of innate and adaptive immune responses, cytokine release, antigen presentation, and leukocyte recruitment, processes that are thought to contribute to secondary brain injury and post-stroke inflammation.

Building on this inflammatory signature, the enrichment profile also highlights pathways related to extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue barrier disruption. Notable examples include extracellular matrix structural constituent (Gene Ontology:0005201, p = 3.81 × 10−8), external encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p = 9.27 × 10−17), matrix metalloproteinases (WikiPathways:129, p = 4.38 × 10−3), and endopeptidase inhibitor activity (Gene Ontology:0004866, p = 5.57 × 10−4). The statistical strength of these terms, particularly external encapsulating structure with a p-value of 9.27 × 10−17 and extracellular matrix structural constituent with a p-value of 3.81 × 10−8, suggests that structural tissue remodeling may be an important component of the observed signal. This interpretation is biologically plausible because extracellular matrix degradation and protease imbalance are well-established contributors to blood-brain barrier breakdown, edema, and hemorrhagic transformation after stroke. In this context, matrix metalloproteinases have been repeatedly implicated in ischemic brain injury in both experimental and clinical settings. In addition, enrichment of the mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04010, p = 3.67 × 10−4) is compatible with the involvement of stress-response signaling cascades that may regulate inflammation, apoptosis, and neuronal survival after cerebral ischemia.

Taken together, these findings suggest a coordinated relationship between inflammatory activation and structural tissue responses. Extending this view, several additional signals may reflect broader cellular adaptations to ischemic stress. For example, the HRD1 complex (Comprehensive Resource of Mammalian Protein Complexes:6859, p = 3.09 × 10−2) and receptor complex (Gene Ontology:0043235, p = 2.58 × 10−7) could indicate altered protein quality control and receptor-mediated signaling under ischemic conditions. At the same time, tissue-enrichment terms involving appendix goblet cells and colon goblet cells from the Human Protein Atlas are more cautiously interpreted, as they likely reflect expression overlap rather than stroke-specific biology. Overall, the pathway landscape is consistent with a model in which stroke is associated with coordinated inflammatory activation, cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix injury, and engagement of stress-response pathways. The very small p-values observed across several terms, including 5.32 × 10−16, 9.27 × 10−17, and 1.03 × 10−8, provide substantial statistical support for these shared mechanisms, while still warranting cautious biological interpretation where pathway specificity is uncertain.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall enrichment landscape in view, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### HRD1 complex (CORUM:6859) 

The HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex is a core endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation machinery that preserves protein quality control within the endoplasmic reticulum by identifying misfolded or incompletely folded proteins, moving them across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane back into the cytosol, attaching ubiquitin, and directing them to proteasomal destruction. Structural and mechanistic studies indicate that this complex is organized around the ubiquitin ligase HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 together with accessory factors that mediate substrate recognition, channel formation, and degradation efficiency. In yeast, the active complex includes HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1, HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 3, degradation in endoplasmic reticulum protein 1, ubiquitin suppressor protein 1, and yeast oligosaccharyltransferase 9, which together create a luminal recognition site for misfolded glycoproteins and a membrane retrotranslocation route formed by paired half channels in a locally thinned membrane region, thereby allowing hydrophilic polypeptide segments to cross the membrane for degradation (PubMed:32327568, PubMed:28682307, PubMed:35970394). In mammals, the most conserved functional counterpart appears to be the suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex, in which suppressor of lin 12 like is required for stable complex assembly, substrate recruitment, and full ligase activity. Genetic and biochemical studies further suggest that disruption of suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 coupling impairs endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation at multiple levels, including substrate handoff, complex formation, and recruitment of ubiquitin conjugating enzymes, and that such defects may compromise organismal viability and contribute to human neurodevelopmental disease (PubMed:41642983, PubMed:38365914, PubMed:37943610). Beyond proteostasis, this pathway also appears to modulate inflammatory signaling by targeting newly synthesized stimulator of interferon genes for degradation under basal conditions, thereby limiting the size of the activable innate immune pool (PubMed:37142791). Taken together, the HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex may be viewed as a proteostasis and signaling checkpoint that integrates endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, degradation of misfolded proteins, and restraint of maladaptive inflammatory activation.

Against this mechanistic background, the relevance of the HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex to stroke can be considered in the context of ischemic and reperfusion stress, during which neurons, glia, and vascular cells experience abrupt disturbances in oxygen supply, energy metabolism, calcium balance, redox state, and protein folding. Although most cited studies define the pathway mechanistically rather than in stroke models, they provide a biologically plausible framework for stroke relevance because failure of suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 mediated endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation causes accumulation of misfolded proteins and heightened cellular stress, processes that are highly pertinent to ischemic brain injury (PubMed:32327568, PubMed:28682307, PubMed:41642983, PubMed:38365914). Human and mouse genetic evidence further indicates that reduced function of this pathway is especially damaging to the nervous system, producing developmental delay, ataxia, and loss of viability, which supports the idea that neural tissue is highly dependent on intact endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation capacity (PubMed:37943610, PubMed:41642983). Most directly, a recent stroke focused study in a chronic kidney disease and stroke model reported that decreased suppressor of lin 12 like expression was associated with altered endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, enhanced endoplasmic reticulum stress, greater cellular death, neurodegeneration, and worsened neurological and cognitive outcomes, while pharmacological inhibition of endoplasmic reticulum stress ameliorated these abnormalities and reduced white matter damage, thereby placing impaired suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 function within a plausible causal chain linking proteostasis failure to aggravated stroke injury (PubMed:40301526). In parallel, the finding that suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 limits stimulator of interferon genes signaling suggests an additional stroke relevant mechanism, because loss of this degradative brake could amplify innate immune and inflammatory responses after ischemia and thereby potentially exacerbate tissue injury and secondary degeneration (PubMed:37142791). Overall, the current literature supports the view that the HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex is related to stroke primarily as a protective endoplasmic reticulum quality control pathway whose dysfunction may intensify ischemia induced proteotoxic stress, inflammatory activation, white matter injury, and post stroke functional decline, particularly in the presence of systemic comorbidities such as chronic kidney disease.[PubMed:32327568](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32327568) [PubMed:28682307](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28682307) [PubMed:35970394](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35970394) [PubMed:37943610](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37943610) [PubMed:41642983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41642983) [PubMed:38365914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38365914) [PubMed:37142791](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37142791) [PubMed:40301526](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40301526) 

With this biological context in place, the enrichment results can be interpreted more coherently in relation to the broader stroke associated protein set.

There were an unspecified number of stroke-associated proteins analyzed in the function enrichment analysis, and these proteins were significantly enriched in the pathway describing the HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex as a core endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation machinery that preserves protein quality control within the endoplasmic reticulum by recognizing misfolded or incompletely folded proteins, transporting them across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane into the cytosol, conjugating ubiquitin, and directing them to proteasomal degradation. Mechanistically, this pathway is supported by structural and biochemical evidence showing that, in yeast, at least 5 core components, namely HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1, HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 3, degradation in endoplasmic reticulum protein 1, ubiquitin suppressor protein 1, and yeast oligosaccharyltransferase 9, cooperate to generate a luminal substrate recognition site and a membrane retrotranslocation route composed of paired half channels within a locally thinned membrane environment, thereby enabling hydrophilic polypeptide segments to traverse the membrane for degradation (PubMed:32327568, PubMed:28682307, PubMed:35970394). In mammals, the most conserved functional counterpart is the suppressor of lin 12 like and HMG CoA reductase degradation protein 1 complex, in which suppressor of lin 12 like is required for stable complex assembly, efficient substrate recruitment, and full ubiquitin ligase activity, while disruption of this coupling has been shown to impair endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation at multiple levels, including substrate transfer, complex formation, and ubiquitin conjugating enzyme recruitment, with consequences that extend to organismal viability and human neurodevelopmental disease (PubMed:41642983, PubMed:38365914, PubMed:37943610). Beyond proteostasis, this pathway also has direct relevance to stroke biology because it restrains inflammatory signaling through degradation of newly synthesized stimulator of interferon genes under basal conditions, thereby limiting the size of the activable innate immune pool, a mechanism that may be particularly important in a disease context characterized by strong sterile inflammatory activation and endoplasmic reticulum stress (PubMed:37142791). Together, these observations suggest that the enriched pathway captures a biologically coherent intersection of protein quality control, endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, ubiquitin dependent degradation, and inflammatory restraint, all of which are highly pertinent to stroke pathophysiology.

Building on the enrichment overview, the following section introduces the significant proteins identified in the analysis in greater detail.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.
Among the functions listed, LTBR stands out as highly relevant to stroke because it occupies a central position in pathways that govern neuroinflammation, innate immune activation, and secondary tissue injury after cerebral ischemia. Stroke pathophysiology is strongly shaped by rapid activation of NF-kappa-B-, MAPK-, and inflammasome-dependent programs in resident brain cells and infiltrating leukocytes, leading to cytokine release, endothelial activation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and progressive neuronal damage. LTBR is particularly notable because it can both amplify and restrain inflammatory signaling depending on context: it promotes Lys-63-linked ubiquitination events that support type I interferon signaling and inflammasome activation, but it also acts as a negative regulator of TLR4-driven NF-kappa-B signaling and suppresses the non-canonical NF-kappa-B pathway through effects on NFKB2 and MAP3K14. This bidirectional regulatory capacity is important in stroke, where excessive inflammation worsens injury, yet complete suppression of immune signaling may impair debris clearance and tissue remodeling. Its connection to TLR4 signaling is especially compelling, because TLR4 is a well-established mediator of sterile inflammation after ischemic stroke. Likewise, regulation of inflammasome activity is highly pertinent given the recognized contribution of ASC-dependent inflammasome assembly to post-stroke neuronal injury and leukocyte recruitment. The described role in bacterial expulsion is less directly linked to stroke itself, but may still be relevant in the context of post-stroke infection susceptibility and systemic immune dysregulation. Overall, LTBR appears to be a mechanistically significant immunoregulatory node whose modulation could influence the balance between detrimental post-ischemic inflammation and adaptive immune repair processes.[PubMed:33148796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33148796) [PubMed:33608556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33608556) [PubMed:25847972](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25847972) [PubMed:27980081](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27980081) [PubMed:27438768](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27438768)

### antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class I (GO:0002474) 

Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via major histocompatibility complex class one is a core cellular immune pathway through which intracellular proteins are degraded into short peptides, loaded onto classical major histocompatibility complex class one molecules, and displayed at the cell surface for surveillance by cluster of differentiation eight positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes. In the canonical route, endogenous proteins are cleaved mainly by the proteasome, including the immunoproteasome under inflammatory conditions, and the resulting peptides are transported into the endoplasmic reticulum by transporter associated with antigen processing, where peptide loading complexes support assembly of major histocompatibility complex class one heavy chain with beta two microglobulin and antigenic peptide before export through the Golgi apparatus to the plasma membrane. The pathway is highly regulated at multiple levels, including transcriptional control of major histocompatibility complex class one molecules and antigen processing machinery by inflammatory signaling such as nuclear factor kappa B and histone acetyltransferases p300 and CREB binding protein, as demonstrated in cancer cells where activation of these regulators increases major histocompatibility complex class one expression, immunoproteasome components, and peptide transport machinery (PubMed:33602823). Beyond direct presentation of endogenous antigens, professional antigen presenting cells, especially dendritic cells, can route exogenous material into major histocompatibility complex class one presentation through cross-presentation, using either cytosolic or vacuolar processing routes and specialized intracellular trafficking steps involving post Golgi compartments and phagosomal export machinery (PubMed:41364771, PubMed:39955774, PubMed:26985398, PubMed:10839810, PubMed:8666786). The pathway is also sensitive to perturbation by infection, cellular stress, and organelle dysfunction: viral proteins can suppress peptide loading or surface display, whereas endoplasmic reticulum stress and Golgi fragmentation can reduce peptide major histocompatibility complex class one complex presentation (PubMed:38483968, PubMed:32755306, PubMed:35087068). Collectively, this pathway links intracellular proteostasis, inflammatory signaling, organelle homeostasis, and adaptive immune activation, thereby shaping whether damaged, infected, transformed, or stressed cells become visible to cytotoxic lymphocytes.  

Against this mechanistic background, the pathway may be cautiously considered in relation to stroke, where sterile injury and immune activation occur in parallel over time. Although the provided publications do not study stroke directly, they define mechanisms that are highly relevant to stroke pathobiology because stroke induces sterile inflammation, neuronal and vascular cell stress, blood brain barrier disruption, antigen release, and subsequent activation of both innate and adaptive immunity. In ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury, damaged neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, microglia, infiltrating macrophages, and dendritic cell like antigen presenting cells are exposed to inflammatory cytokines and danger signals that are expected to enhance major histocompatibility complex class one antigen processing and presentation machinery, particularly through pathways involving nuclear factor kappa B, signal transducer and activator of transcription one, and immunoproteasome induction. This inference is supported by studies showing that inflammatory transcriptional programs can strongly increase major histocompatibility complex class one antigen presentation capacity, including upregulation of major histocompatibility complex class one molecules, immunoproteasome subunits, and peptide transport machinery (PubMed:33602823, PubMed:36977556, PubMed:38605963). In the post stroke brain, such enhancement would be expected to increase display of self peptides derived from injured intracellular proteins, thereby facilitating recognition by cytotoxic T lymphocytes and potentially amplifying secondary tissue injury. At the same time, cross-presentation mechanisms characterized in dendritic cells provide a plausible route by which brain derived antigens released from dying cells are captured in cervical lymphoid tissues or by infiltrating antigen presenting cells and then presented on major histocompatibility complex class one to prime cytotoxic T cell responses (PubMed:41364771, PubMed:39955774, PubMed:26985398, PubMed:10839810, PubMed:8666786). This process is particularly relevant to delayed neuroinflammation after stroke, when peripheral adaptive immunity contributes to lesion evolution and repair. The publications also indicate that endoplasmic reticulum stress and Golgi disorganization suppress major histocompatibility complex class one peptide display (PubMed:32755306), a finding of special importance in stroke because ischemia, reperfusion, oxidative stress, and excitotoxicity profoundly disturb endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi homeostasis; thus, stroke may produce spatially and temporally heterogeneous antigen presentation, with some cells becoming more immunogenic through inflammatory induction while others lose efficient peptide loading because of severe organelle injury. In addition, studies of viral immune evasion and peptide loading complex arrest illustrate how disruption of transporter associated with antigen processing dependent loading changes cell surface major histocompatibility complex class one expression (PubMed:35087068, PubMed:38483968), which is conceptually relevant because similar defects could emerge in severely injured brain cells after stroke. Overall, this pathway is related to stroke through its central role in converting intracellular damage caused by cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage into adaptive immune recognition: it can promote cytotoxic lymphocyte activation against brain antigens, shape the magnitude and persistence of post stroke neuroinflammation, and influence the balance between harmful immune mediated secondary injury and beneficial clearance of damaged tissue.[PubMed:33602823](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33602823) [PubMed:41364771](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41364771) [PubMed:39955774](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39955774) [PubMed:38605963](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38605963) [PubMed:35087068](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35087068) [PubMed:26985398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26985398) [PubMed:10839810](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10839810) [PubMed:36977556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36977556) [PubMed:38483968](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38483968) [PubMed:32755306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32755306) [PubMed:8666786](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8666786) 

Building on this biological context, the enrichment result suggests that this pathway is represented in the analyzed stroke related dataset by a small but potentially informative protein set. There were 4 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via major histocompatibility complex class one, indicating that this immune presentation program is represented by a compact but potentially biologically meaningful protein set within the analyzed stroke-related dataset. This pathway describes a quantitatively important surveillance system in which intracellular proteins are proteolytically processed into short peptides, transferred into the endoplasmic reticulum, assembled with major histocompatibility complex class one heavy chain and beta two microglobulin, and then transported to the cell surface for recognition by cluster of differentiation eight positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes; notably, the pathway is further modulated by inflammatory transcriptional control and organelle stress responses, with prior studies showing that activation of nuclear factor kappa B together with histone acetyltransferases p300 and CREB binding protein can increase major histocompatibility complex class one expression, immunoproteasome components, and peptide transport machinery (PubMed:33602823), while specialized cross-presentation routes in dendritic cells expand the range of antigens entering this pathway through cytosolic and vacuolar mechanisms involving post Golgi trafficking and phagosomal export steps (PubMed:41364771, PubMed:39955774, PubMed:26985398, PubMed:10839810, PubMed:8666786), and viral interference, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and Golgi fragmentation can each measurably reduce peptide major histocompatibility complex class one complex presentation efficiency (PubMed:38483968, PubMed:32755306, PubMed:35087068). We also include the protein-protein interaction network visualization together with the direct link to the STRING webpage to support inspection of the 4-protein interaction landscape in stroke.

To further clarify how this enrichment signal may connect to stroke biology, the significant proteins are introduced below in the same order as in the draft. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

IFI30 is the protein that most clearly stands out as potentially relevant to stroke because its core function lies at the interface of lysosomal processing, antigen presentation, and adaptive immune activation. Post-stroke pathology is increasingly understood to involve not only acute ischemic injury but also a substantial secondary immune component, including activation of microglia/macrophages, processing of damage-associated antigens, and recruitment of T-cell responses. By promoting reduction of disulfide bond-containing proteins in endolysosomal compartments, IFI30 may enhance the presentation of self or injury-derived antigens after cerebral ischemia, thereby influencing neuroinflammation and possibly chronic immune-mediated tissue remodeling. Its additional role in cross-presentation is particularly notable because this mechanism can link innate sensing of tissue damage to cluster of differentiation eight positive T-cell activation, a pathway that may contribute to delayed neuronal injury or post-stroke immune dysregulation. Thus, although IFI30 is not a canonical stroke gene, its biology is highly relevant to immune mechanisms that shape infarct evolution and recovery.  

In a related but distinct way, ULBP2 may connect cellular stress signals to immune effector activation in the setting of stroke. ULBP2 is also highly relevant to stroke because it represents a molecular link between cellular stress and cytotoxic immune activation. Ischemic stroke induces profound metabolic stress, oxidative injury, and inflammatory signaling in neurons, glia, and vascular cells, conditions that can favor expression of stress ligands such as ULBP2. Through activation of natural killer cells and amplification of cluster of differentiation eight positive T-cell responses, ULBP2-related pathways could contribute to post-stroke neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier injury, and secondary cell death via perforin- and cytokine-dependent mechanisms, including tumor necrosis factor alpha production. This is particularly important because sterile inflammation after stroke often co-opts immune pathways that normally function in antiviral or antitumor surveillance. Therefore, ULBP2 stands out as a plausible mediator of immune recognition of stressed ischemic tissue, with potential implications for infarct progression and systemic immune alterations after stroke.

### Appendix; goblet cells[≥Low] (HPA:0030891) 

The pathway term "Appendix; goblet cells[greater than or equal to Low]" most plausibly refers to the presence or relative abundance of goblet cells within appendiceal mucosa at or above a low threshold. Goblet cells are specialized secretory epithelial cells distributed throughout the intestinal tract, including the appendix, and their principal function is the production and secretion of mucins that form the protective mucus layer overlying the intestinal epithelium. This mucus barrier limits direct contact between luminal microbes and the mucosal surface, supports epithelial integrity, and contributes to immune homeostasis. In the appendix, goblet cells are a prominent epithelial lineage and are relevant both to normal barrier physiology and to appendiceal pathological states, including mucinous neoplasms and goblet cell adenocarcinoma. Although most of the provided literature on appendiceal goblet cells concerns neoplastic classification rather than cerebrovascular disease, the broader biological role of goblet cells in maintaining intestinal barrier function appears directly relevant to stroke because intestinal barrier disruption after cerebral ischemia may amplify systemic inflammation. Thus, this pathway may be interpreted less as an appendix-specific oncological marker in stroke and more as a surrogate of mucin-producing epithelial barrier competence within the gut-associated immune axis.

Building on this interpretation, the available evidence suggests that the relationship between goblet cells and stroke is mediated through the gut barrier and systemic inflammation rather than through appendiceal neoplasia. Among the provided studies, the most directly relevant report demonstrated in an experimental model of ischemic stroke that stroke increased gut mast cells, enhanced histamine signaling, elevated circulating inflammatory mediators, and was accompanied by a significant reduction in mucin-producing goblet cells together with loss of gut barrier integrity; these effects were especially pronounced in aged animals, thereby linking depletion of goblet cells to post-stroke intestinal inflammation and peripheral immune activation (PubMed:32429999). This finding is biologically important because goblet cells sustain the mucus layer that restrains microbial and inflammatory translocation from the intestinal lumen into the circulation. Therefore, a pathway reflecting goblet cell presence in the appendix or gut mucosa may be relevant to stroke as an indicator of preserved mucosal defense, whereas reduced goblet cell abundance would be expected to favor barrier failure, exaggerated systemic cytokine release, microbiota disturbance, and potentially worse neurological recovery after ischemic injury. By contrast, the remaining publications primarily describe goblet cell adenocarcinoma and other appendiceal neoplasms, which clarify the epithelial identity and pathological significance of appendiceal goblet cells but do not provide direct evidence for a causal role in stroke. Taken together, the literature supports a stroke connection for this pathway through post-ischemic gut inflammation, loss of mucin-producing goblet cells, and consequent impairment of intestinal barrier function, rather than through appendix-specific tumor biology.[PubMed:32429999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32429999) 

Consistent with this biological framework, there were 20 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway term “Appendix; goblet cells[greater than or equal to Low],” a signal that is most plausibly interpreted as reflecting mucin-producing epithelial barrier competence rather than an appendix-specific disease process. In the context of stroke, this enrichment may be biologically relevant because goblet cells are major contributors to intestinal mucus production, epithelial protection, and host-microbe separation, and disruption of these barrier functions after cerebral ischemia can intensify systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation. Therefore, the presence of 20 enriched proteins supports a quantitatively substantial connection between stroke biology and the gut-associated epithelial defense axis. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 20 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network inspection.

With this enrichment pattern in mind, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help explain how this pathway could intersect with stroke-related biology. We introduce them in detail below.

Among the listed proteins, BSG stands out as one of the most directly relevant to stroke because it is tightly linked to axon integrity, neuron-glia interactions, and post-injury neuronal survival. Stroke causes acute neuronal injury followed by secondary white matter damage, axonal degeneration, and limited regenerative sprouting. In this context, the reported role of BSG in maintaining normal myelination and preventing degeneration of myelinated axons is highly pertinent, particularly for ischemic injury affecting white matter tracts. Its anti-apoptotic effect on motoneurons further supports a potentially neuroprotective relevance in the setting of ischemic or post-stroke degeneration. At the same time, BSG is also a negative regulator of neurite outgrowth via RTN4R/RTN4RL2 and ganglioside-dependent mechanisms, which may be important for understanding why axonal regeneration after stroke is often incomplete. Thus, BSG is mechanistically interesting because it may contribute both to preservation of axonal structure and to restriction of regenerative plasticity after injury, two central features of stroke pathobiology.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Shifting from axonal maintenance to vascular remodeling, COL18A1 is also highly relevant to stroke because vascular remodeling and post-ischemic angiogenesis are major determinants of tissue recovery. The anti-angiogenic function described here, especially the inhibition of VEGFA-driven endothelial proliferation and migration, directly intersects with one of the principal repair programs activated after cerebral ischemia. VEGFA signaling contributes to both beneficial neovascularization and, in some contexts, blood-brain barrier instability; therefore, an endogenous inhibitor such as COL18A1 may substantially shape the balance between vascular repair and maladaptive remodeling. Its capacity to modulate endothelial migration via integrin-dependent pathways further strengthens its relevance, since endothelial motility and matrix interactions are essential for vessel sprouting and reperfusion in peri-infarct tissue. Accordingly, COL18A1 should be considered an important regulator of the vascular response to stroke, with possible implications for infarct evolution, collateral remodeling, and recovery.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

Extending this discussion from vascular remodeling to cellular energetics, CHCHD10 is notable in the context of stroke because mitochondrial integrity is central to ischemic brain injury. During cerebral ischemia and reperfusion, failure of oxidative phosphorylation, disruption of mitochondrial ultrastructure, and collapse of cristae architecture contribute to energy depletion, oxidative stress, and activation of cell death pathways. A protein implicated in maintaining mitochondrial organization and cristae structure is therefore mechanistically relevant even though the provided annotation is concise. In neurons, which are highly dependent on mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate production, disturbances in such structural maintenance could exacerbate susceptibility to ischemic injury. CHCHD10 may thus represent a candidate modifier of neuronal resilience, particularly in relation to bioenergetic failure and apoptotic signaling after stroke.

From mitochondrial stress responses, the analysis then moves toward systemic and central adaptive signaling. Although this entry is labeled as GDF15, the described function corresponds to its receptor GFRAL, a stress-responsive brainstem signaling node. This pathway is potentially relevant to stroke because systemic and central stress responses are prominent after acute cerebrovascular injury. Brainstem circuits controlling appetite, autonomic adaptation, and sickness behavior are often altered in severe stroke, and stress-induced GDF15 signaling may contribute to anorexia, metabolic dysregulation, and catabolic states that influence recovery. The activation of RET-dependent MAPK and AKT signaling also suggests a broader role in neuronal stress signaling. While the connection to stroke is more indirect than for vascular or axonal proteins, this pathway is noteworthy because post-stroke outcomes are strongly affected by systemic metabolic adaptation, nutritional decline, and neurohumoral stress responses.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

A related but distinct aspect of post-stroke adaptation involves stress-responsive ribonucleic acid metabolism and vascular signaling. This protein is relevant to stroke because it links two important biological themes in ischemic injury: stress-responsive ribonucleic acid metabolism and angiogenesis. Angiogenin has dual importance in tissue injury, being implicated in both adaptive stress responses and vascular remodeling. By restraining ANG differently in the cytoplasm and nucleus depending on stress conditions, this inhibitor may shape whether cells undergo protective translational reprogramming, cytotoxic ribonucleic acid cleavage, or angiogenic signaling. Its additional association with redox homeostasis further increases its relevance, since oxidative stress is a core mediator of ischemia-reperfusion damage. Therefore, this protein may influence both neuronal survival pathways and the vascular repair response after stroke, making it a biologically interesting candidate despite the absence of direct stroke-specific annotation in the provided text.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170) 

In parallel with these intracellular stress pathways, extracellular proteolytic control may also be relevant to post-stroke tissue injury. WFDC2 is potentially relevant to stroke because protease activity is a major determinant of blood-brain barrier disruption, extracellular matrix degradation, inflammation, and hemorrhagic transformation after ischemic injury. Although the provided annotation is brief, a broad-range protease inhibitor could plausibly modulate proteolytic cascades that influence edema formation, leukocyte infiltration, and tissue remodeling. In stroke biology, endogenous antiprotease systems are often protective because excessive protease activation worsens vascular leakage and secondary injury. Thus, WFDC2 is noteworthy as a candidate regulator of post-stroke neurovascular integrity, even if the current functional description does not specify the exact protease targets involved.

Closely related to neurovascular integrity, junctional organization is another process that may shape barrier stability after stroke. LGALS4 may have relevance to stroke through its putative role in adherens junction assembly. Junctional integrity is fundamental for maintaining vascular barriers, including the blood-brain barrier, whose breakdown is a hallmark of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. Although LGALS4 is better known in epithelial contexts, proteins that regulate cell-cell adhesion and glycan-dependent membrane organization can influence barrier stability, inflammatory cell trafficking, and tissue repair. Therefore, LGALS4 is of interest as a possible modulator of junctional architecture and permeability-related processes that are central to stroke pathogenesis, even if the available annotation does not establish a direct cerebrovascular role.

Finally, beyond local neurovascular mechanisms, systemic metabolic regulation may provide an additional layer of relevance for this enriched pathway. FABP1 is indirectly relevant to stroke because lipid handling and systemic metabolic status are major contributors to cerebrovascular risk and recovery. Its role in hepatocellular cholesterol uptake and intracellular lipid trafficking places it within pathways that influence dyslipidemia and atherosclerosis, both major upstream drivers of ischemic stroke. In addition, altered lipid metabolism after stroke can affect inflammatory responses and energy balance. While FABP1 is not a direct mediator of neurovascular injury in the provided annotation, it stands out as a plausible contributor to stroke susceptibility through systemic metabolic mechanisms, particularly those related to lipid homeostasis and vascular risk burden.

### endopeptidase inhibitor activity (GO:0004866) 

Endopeptidase inhibitor activity refers to the molecular function by which a protein, peptide, antibody, or small molecule binds to an endopeptidase and suppresses its catalytic activity. Endopeptidases cleave peptide bonds within target proteins and thereby regulate coagulation, fibrinolysis, extracellular matrix turnover, inflammatory signaling, blood vessel integrity, and cell death. In the context of cerebrovascular disease, this activity is especially important because several biologically central enzymes in stroke are endopeptidases, including coagulation proteases such as activated factor eleven and thrombin, fibrinolytic proteases such as tissue plasminogen activator, and matrix metalloproteinases such as matrix metalloproteinase three. Endogenous inhibitors within this functional space include serpin family members such as plasminogen activator inhibitor one, neuroserpin, antithrombin, and complement-related protease inhibitors, whereas therapeutic inhibitors include monoclonal antibodies, direct oral anticoagulants, reversal agents, and selective metalloproteinase inhibitors. The pathway is therefore not a single linear cascade, but rather a broader regulatory principle that restrains proteolysis in blood and brain. In stroke biology, this balance is crucial because insufficient inhibition of endopeptidases can promote thrombosis, blood brain barrier disruption, hemorrhagic transformation, and neuroinflammation, whereas excessive inhibition can impair thrombus resolution or alter hemostatic protection. Accordingly, endopeptidase inhibitor activity has relevance to both ischemic stroke prevention and acute or subacute brain injury after stroke.  

Against this mechanistic background, the published literature collectively suggests that endopeptidase inhibitor activity is closely linked to stroke through two major and partially opposing mechanisms: regulation of thrombus formation in the circulation and limitation of protease-mediated injury within the ischemic brain. On the prevention side, inhibition of coagulation endopeptidases modifies cardioembolic stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. Activated factor eleven inhibition reduced bleeding but did not provide equivalent protection from stroke compared with established anticoagulation, as shown by the premature termination of the asundexian trial because stroke or systemic embolism was more frequent with asundexian than with apixaban, despite fewer major bleeding events, and similar patterns were observed across prior oral anticoagulant exposure strata, indicating that selective suppression of this protease may alter the efficacy-safety balance in stroke prevention rather than simply improve it (PubMed:39225267; PubMed:40136309). By contrast, inhibition of factor eleven with abelacimab markedly lowered bleeding relative to rivaroxaban, supporting the concept that targeting coagulation proteases remains mechanistically important for stroke prevention, although definitive protection from ischemic events still appears to require careful validation (PubMed:39842011).  

A complementary line of evidence points from the circulation to the neurovascular unit, where endopeptidase inhibitor activity may be protective when it restrains proteases that damage the blood brain barrier or amplify inflammatory injury. Matrix metalloproteinase three, a zinc-dependent endopeptidase, was identified as a mediator of vascular injury, edema, and hemorrhagic transformation, particularly in hyperglycemic and diabetic stroke models, and its inhibition improved functional outcome and reduced vascular damage, highlighting the potential role of protease inhibition in preserving cerebrovascular integrity after ischemia and reperfusion (Stroke abstracts on matrix metalloproteinase three inhibition; PubMed:39419277). A particularly strong example is the compartmentalized control of tissue plasminogen activator by distinct endogenous inhibitors: neuroserpin limits harmful tissue plasminogen activator activity in the central nervous system and preserves blood brain barrier function, whereas plasminogen activator inhibitor one restrains intravascular fibrinolysis. Experimental evidence showed that neuroserpin deficiency worsened infarct size, blood brain barrier permeability, and spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, while plasminogen activator inhibitor one deficiency improved cerebral blood flow recovery and reduced infarct size, demonstrating that the biological effect of endopeptidase inhibition depends on where the target protease acts (PubMed:35122213). Reviews further support neuroserpin as a neuroprotective inhibitor that may extend the safe therapeutic window of thrombolysis and reduce inflammation and barrier disruption after stroke (PubMed:39191396; PubMed:33032511). Clinical studies on idarucizumab, a reversal agent for dabigatran, also illustrate the translational importance of controlling endopeptidase-related coagulation pathways in acute stroke care, because rapid neutralization of anticoagulant effect can restore eligibility for thrombolysis in ischemic stroke and may improve management of hemorrhagic presentations (PubMed:36295516; PubMed:36738375). More broadly, systematic synthesis of serpin studies concluded that serpin family proteins are altered in stroke patients and that several protease inhibitors show therapeutic benefit in experimental ischemic stroke, reinforcing the view that endopeptidase inhibitor activity is a central determinant of stroke onset, progression, and treatment response (PubMed:37017398).[PubMed:39225267](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39225267) [PubMed:40136309](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40136309) [PubMed:39842011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39842011) [PubMed:39419277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39419277) [PubMed:35122213](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35122213) [PubMed:39191396](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39191396) [PubMed:33032511](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33032511) [PubMed:36295516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36295516) [PubMed:36738375](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36738375) [PubMed:37017398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37017398) 

Consistent with this literature context, there were 8 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of endopeptidase inhibitor activity. This functional category captures a quantitatively important regulatory layer in cerebrovascular biology because it governs suppression of proteolytic enzymes that act within proteins rather than at terminal peptide bonds, thereby influencing multiple stroke-relevant processes including coagulation, fibrinolysis, extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory signaling, vascular permeability, and cell death. In the setting of stroke, the biological relevance of this enrichment appears high because dysregulated protease inhibition can shift the balance toward thrombosis, blood brain barrier failure, hemorrhagic transformation, and secondary neuroinflammatory injury, whereas excessive inhibition may reduce thrombus clearance and alter hemostatic stability. The identification of 8 proteins within this enriched function therefore supports the interpretation that proteolytic restraint is not a marginal feature, but a central molecular principle linked to both ischemic stroke pathogenesis and post-stroke tissue injury.

To place these 8 proteins into a network context, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network interrogation and evidence review.  
![PPI Network](imgs/efa30ec3-8d09-404f-9700-2d78b728c5a1.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=D504CB3BD3AFA557)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Beginning with proteins that may connect most directly to coagulation and inflammatory protease control, AMBP is particularly relevant to stroke because its annotated activity directly intersects with coagulation, a central determinant of ischemic stroke pathogenesis and secondary thrombus propagation. By inhibiting factor ten a and prothrombin activation, AMBP has potential anticoagulant properties, suggesting a plausible role in limiting thrombin generation and fibrin clot formation. Such functions are mechanistically important in thromboembolic stroke, where dysregulated coagulation promotes cerebral vessel occlusion. In addition, inhibition of mast cell proteases may be relevant to post-stroke neurovascular inflammation, blood-brain barrier injury, and tissue remodeling, since mast cell activation has been implicated in acute cerebrovascular damage. Therefore, AMBP stands out as a protein with a dual connection to stroke biology through both hemostatic regulation and inflammatory protease control.  

Shifting from coagulation toward immune and matrix-regulatory mechanisms, BST2 is notable in the context of stroke primarily because it integrates antiviral defense, interferon biology, nuclear factor kappa light chain enhancer of activated B cells signaling, and matrix-remodeling pathways, all of which are relevant to cerebrovascular disease. Viral infection and systemic inflammation can precipitate stroke and worsen outcomes, and BST2 is a broad-spectrum restriction factor active against multiple enveloped viruses, including influenza A virus and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus, both of which have recognized vascular and thromboinflammatory consequences. Beyond antiviral restriction, BST2 influences innate immune signaling by regulating interferon responses and nuclear factor kappa light chain enhancer of activated B cells activation, pathways strongly implicated in endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, and post-ischemic neuroinflammation. Its reported suppression of matrix metalloproteinase fourteen activity is also potentially important, because matrix metalloproteinases contribute to blood-brain barrier breakdown, hemorrhagic transformation, and extracellular matrix remodeling after stroke. Thus, BST2 stands out as a multifunctional immune-regulatory protein that may connect infection-triggered vascular injury with inflammatory and proteolytic mechanisms relevant to stroke progression.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328)  

In a related but somewhat broader protease-regulatory context, CST3 is one of the strongest stroke-relevant candidates in this list because regulation of cysteine proteases is closely linked to vascular remodeling, extracellular matrix turnover, inflammation, and neuronal injury. In the setting of stroke, protease imbalance can contribute to blood-brain barrier disruption, cell death, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. As an endogenous inhibitor of cysteine proteases, CST3 may help restrain excessive proteolytic activity within the neurovascular unit. This is particularly relevant because protease-driven injury is implicated in both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, including edema formation and post-ischemic degeneration. More broadly, CST3 has long been of interest in cerebrovascular and vascular biology as a marker and potential mediator of vascular dysfunction, making its protease-inhibitory role especially meaningful for stroke-related mechanisms.  

The next protein requires somewhat more cautious interpretation because of an apparent annotation mismatch. Although the annotation provided under PI3 appears functionally more consistent with a receptor tyrosine kinase than with the classical PI3 elafin protease inhibitor, the listed signaling activities nonetheless intersect with several pathways that are highly relevant to stroke biology. In particular, phosphoinositide three kinase protein kinase B mechanistic target of rapamycin and signal transducer and activator of transcription three signaling are major determinants of cell survival, inflammation, endothelial behavior, and tissue repair after cerebral ischemia. Activation of these pathways can influence neuronal resistance to injury, glial responses, angiogenesis, and vascular remodeling. Mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling also contributes to ischemic damage and recovery, depending on context and timing. Therefore, despite the apparent annotation inconsistency, the described function may still highlight a signaling axis of potential importance for stroke through regulation of survival and reparative responses in vascular and neural tissues.[PubMed:32499443](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32499443) 

Moving to a protein with a more limited and indirect connection, SPINK1 has a less direct connection to stroke than several other proteins in this panel. However, one potentially relevant aspect is its reported modulation of nitric oxide production. Nitric oxide is a critical regulator of vascular tone, platelet function, endothelial homeostasis, and cerebral blood flow, all of which are central to stroke pathophysiology. Even so, the annotation provided is highly specific to the male reproductive tract, and therefore the evidence for a meaningful stroke-related role from this description alone appears limited. SPINK1 would thus be considered a lower-priority candidate unless additional context indicates expression or activity in vascular, inflammatory, or neural compartments relevant to cerebrovascular disease.[PubMed:14645103](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14645103) [PubMed:16083722](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16083722) [PubMed:22228629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22228629) [PubMed:9828198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9828198) 

By comparison, SPINT2 appears somewhat more plausibly connected to post-stroke repair pathways. SPINT2 is potentially relevant to stroke because it participates in protease-dependent activation of hepatocyte growth factor and downstream mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, both of which have recognized roles in tissue protection, angiogenesis, and repair. Hepatocyte growth factor is widely studied as a neurotrophic and vasculoprotective factor that may reduce ischemic injury, support endothelial integrity, and promote recovery after stroke. Consequently, proteins that regulate hepatocyte growth factor activation can influence the magnitude and timing of these reparative responses. In addition, protease regulation itself is important in stroke, where excessive proteolysis contributes to barrier disruption and inflammatory injury. Although the annotation is not explicitly cerebrovascular, SPINT2 stands out as a plausible modulator of growth factor signaling relevant to post-stroke neurovascular remodeling.[PubMed:20977675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20977675) [PubMed:28710277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28710277) [PubMed:34562451](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34562451) 

Among the proteins in this set, TIMP1 may have one of the clearest links to established stroke mechanisms. TIMP1 is one of the most compelling stroke-related proteins in this list because matrix metalloproteinases are central mediators of blood-brain barrier disruption, leukocyte infiltration, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, and post-ischemic extracellular matrix remodeling. In particular, excessive matrix metalloproteinase activity, especially matrix metalloproteinase two and matrix metalloproteinase nine, has been strongly linked to acute ischemic brain injury and secondary vascular damage. By inhibiting a broad spectrum of matrix metalloproteinases, TIMP1 may function as an endogenous protective regulator of neurovascular integrity. Its additional signaling roles through CD63 and integrins further suggest influence on cell survival, migration, and tissue repair, which are important during recovery and remodeling after stroke. Therefore, TIMP1 stands out as a highly relevant candidate connecting protease control with both acute injury limitation and longer-term reparative processes.  

Finally, WFDC2 may be relevant to stroke at a general mechanistic level because broad protease inhibition can modulate inflammatory injury, extracellular matrix degradation, and tissue remodeling, all of which are important components of stroke pathology. Protease excess contributes to neurovascular unit damage, blood-brain barrier breakdown, and secondary degeneration after cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage. However, compared with proteins such as TIMP1, AMBP, or CST3, the annotation for WFDC2 is relatively nonspecific and does not identify a direct connection to coagulation, matrix metalloproteinases, or canonical cerebrovascular signaling pathways. Thus, while WFDC2 remains of potential interest as a regulator of proteolytic balance, the evidence provided here supports it as a secondary rather than primary stroke-relevant candidate.

### Colon; goblet cells[High] (HPA:0130893) 

The pathway denoted as colon goblet cells high refers to a transcriptionally and functionally enriched state of colonic goblet cells, which are specialized secretory epithelial cells responsible for producing mucins that organize the colonic mucus barrier. Recent work has shown that colonic goblet cells are not a uniform population, but instead comprise anatomically and molecularly distinct subsets with different barrier functions. In particular, intercrypt goblet cells located on the luminal surface between crypt openings produce a specialized mucus that complements crypt-derived mucus plumes, together forming a net-like barrier that prevents bacterial access to the epithelium while still allowing selective permeability to small molecules. Loss or dysfunction of these highly active goblet cell populations disrupts mucus architecture, exposes the epithelial surface to microbes, and predisposes to intestinal inflammation and colitis. Taken together, this pathway can be understood as a barrier-maintaining epithelial program centered on mucin production, mucus organization, epithelial protection, and regulation of host-microbiota interactions in the colon. Because the intestinal mucus layer is a major determinant of gut permeability, microbial containment, and mucosal immune tone, perturbation of high goblet cell states in the colon may have important systemic consequences that extend beyond the intestine.  

With this biological context in place, the potential connection to stroke appears most plausibly through intestinal barrier dysfunction and systemic inflammatory signaling rather than through a canonical cerebral ischemia pathway. Although the cited literature does not identify colon goblet cells high as a canonical cerebral ischemia signaling pathway, the available evidence supports its possible relevance to stroke through the gut-brain axis. Experimental cerebral ischemia induces intestinal dysbiosis, impairs epithelial tight junction integrity, alters villus and crypt structure, and reduces mucin-producing goblet cells in the colon, indicating that stroke is accompanied by breakdown of the mucus barrier program maintained by highly active goblet cells. In a rat model of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion, treatment with probiotic-derived cell-free supernatant or live probiotic organisms restored the number of colonic mucin-producing goblet cells, improved expression of tight junction proteins, reduced systemic and cerebral inflammatory mediators, and ameliorated neurological deficits and infarct burden, thereby linking preservation of goblet cell-associated barrier function with improved stroke outcome. A related mouse study of post-stroke depression further showed that modulation of the gut microbiota by fecal microbiota transplantation increased goblet cells in the colon while reducing inflammation in both gut and brain and improving behavioral outcomes, again suggesting that restoration of goblet cell-dependent mucosal homeostasis may mitigate post-stroke neuropsychiatric sequelae. Mechanistically, this connection is biologically plausible because high-functioning colonic goblet cells are essential for constructing the protective mucus network that separates microbes from the epithelium; when this goblet cell compartment is reduced or dysfunctional, gaps in the mucus barrier permit microbial and inflammatory stimulation of the intestinal surface, promoting local and systemic inflammation. Such barrier failure could plausibly amplify the circulating inflammatory signals already known to worsen cerebral injury after stroke. Thus, the most coherent interpretation of the current evidence is that the colon goblet cells high pathway may be related to stroke as a protective intestinal barrier program whose disruption contributes to post-stroke gut barrier dysfunction, inflammation, and adverse neurological outcomes, whereas its restoration appears to support recovery.[PubMed:33859001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33859001) [PubMed:38656733](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38656733) [PubMed:40189067](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40189067) 

This broader interpretation is also consistent with the enrichment results obtained from the stroke-associated protein set. There were 13 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway denoted as colon goblet cells high, a barrier-maintaining epithelial program centered on mucin production, mucus organization, epithelial protection, and regulation of host-microbiota interactions in the colon. This enrichment indicates that, within the stroke-related protein set, a measurable subset maps to biological functions linked to intestinal mucus barrier integrity, epithelial-microbial segregation, and mucosal immune homeostasis. Quantitatively, the presence of 13 enriched proteins suggests that this is not an isolated signal, but rather a detectable component of the broader stroke-related molecular landscape, especially because disruption of these processes can increase gut permeability, alter microbial containment, and amplify systemic inflammatory signaling with potential consequences for stroke pathobiology.  

To further contextualize this enrichment, the interaction structure of these proteins is shown below. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 13 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct inspection of interaction evidence and network structure.  
![PPI Network](imgs/f9054727-33d4-4309-a2b6-1481b4e8de94.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=C86BFED649A761A4)

Building on this network-level view, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a more mechanistic manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, BSG stands out as one of the most directly relevant to stroke because its annotated functions converge on several core mechanisms of post-stroke injury and recovery, including axonal integrity, neuronal survival, and regenerative plasticity. Stroke, particularly ischemic stroke, induces secondary white matter injury, axonal degeneration, and neuronal apoptosis; therefore, a molecule required to maintain myelinated axons and protect neurons against apoptosis is of substantial mechanistic interest. The reported role of BSG in preventing degeneration of myelinated axons in adults suggests a potential contribution to preservation of white matter tracts after ischemic or hemorrhagic injury. At the same time, BSG is also described as a negative regulator of neurite outgrowth, acting through RTN4R and RTN4RL2 and ganglioside-dependent pathways. This inhibitory effect is also relevant to stroke because neurological recovery depends in part on axonal sprouting and circuit remodeling in peri-infarct tissue. Thus, BSG may have a dual role in stroke pathobiology: beneficial in maintaining axonal and neuronal viability during injury, but potentially restrictive for regenerative outgrowth during recovery. This combination of neuroprotective and growth-inhibitory properties makes BSG particularly noteworthy as a candidate mediator of both acute damage responses and chronic repair limitation after stroke.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

In comparison with BSG, the next proteins appear to connect to stroke through somewhat different biological dimensions, ranging from mitochondrial maintenance to tissue remodeling and systemic metabolism. CHCHD10 is highly relevant to stroke because mitochondrial integrity is central to ischemic brain injury. During stroke, interruption of oxygen and glucose supply rapidly impairs oxidative phosphorylation, disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential, increases reactive oxygen species generation, and promotes apoptotic and necrotic cell death. A protein implicated in the maintenance of mitochondrial organization and cristae architecture may therefore influence cellular resilience to ischemic stress. Cristae structure is essential for efficient respiratory chain function and adenosine triphosphate production, and its disruption is a recognized feature of neuronal injury after cerebral ischemia. Although the functional annotation provided here is concise and does not include stroke-specific experimental citations, the biological role of CHCHD10 places it within a pathway of major pathogenic importance in stroke, especially in neurons and other metabolically vulnerable cells.  

Extending from mitochondrial homeostasis to post-injury tissue responses, CKAP4 has a less direct connection with stroke than the leading candidates in this list, but it may still be of interest because receptor-mediated antiproliferative signaling can influence tissue remodeling responses after injury. Stroke recovery involves coordinated responses of endothelial cells, glia, and other stromal elements, including proliferation, scar formation, and vascular remodeling. A receptor that transduces antiproliferative signals could theoretically modulate these processes. However, based on the present annotation, the evidence linking CKAP4 specifically to stroke mechanisms is limited, and it appears less immediately compelling than proteins involved in neuronal survival, mitochondrial homeostasis, oxidative stress, or protease regulation.  

At a broader systemic level, FABP1 is potentially relevant to stroke primarily through metabolic and vascular mechanisms rather than direct neural effects. Lipid handling, cholesterol trafficking, and fatty acid metabolism are strongly linked to atherosclerosis, dyslipidemia, and cardiometabolic risk, all of which are major determinants of ischemic stroke susceptibility. By participating in hepatocellular cholesterol uptake and intracellular lipid transport, FABP1 may contribute to the broader metabolic environment that shapes cerebrovascular risk. In addition, altered lipid metabolism can influence inflammation and oxidative stress, which are important in both stroke predisposition and secondary injury. Nevertheless, compared with proteins directly involved in neuronal integrity or post-ischemic tissue damage, FABP1 is better viewed as an indirect stroke-relevant factor.  

A related barrier-oriented perspective also supports consideration of LGALS4, although the evidence remains indirect. LGALS4 may have a plausible relevance to stroke because cell-cell junctional integrity is critical for epithelial and endothelial barrier function. In the context of cerebrovascular disease, disruption of intercellular junctions contributes to blood-brain barrier breakdown, edema formation, and inflammatory cell infiltration after stroke. A lectin involved in adherens junction assembly could therefore be conceptually linked to vascular barrier stability and tissue integrity. However, the current annotation does not establish a brain-specific or stroke-specific role, so LGALS4 should be considered a secondary candidate whose relevance is based on general barrier biology rather than direct evidence in ischemic injury.  

Among the remaining proteins, RNASE1 is especially notable because it intersects with stress adaptation, redox balance, and vascular responses that are all highly pertinent to stroke biology. RNASE1 is one of the most interesting proteins in this list for stroke-related interpretation because its functions intersect with two major dimensions of stroke biology: oxidative stress and angiogenin-dependent stress responses. Cerebral ischemia triggers profound redox imbalance, and proteins involved in redox homeostasis can shape cell survival, inflammatory signaling, and reperfusion injury. In addition, the regulation of angiogenin is particularly noteworthy. Angiogenin has context-dependent roles in stress adaptation, ribonucleic acid metabolism, and angiogenesis, all of which are highly relevant after stroke. The annotation indicates that RNASE1 restrains angiogenin cytotoxic ribonuclease activity in the cytoplasm under basal conditions, but redistributes under stress in a way that alters angiogenin activity across cellular compartments. This suggests that RNASE1 may participate in the molecular switch between homeostasis and injury responses during ischemia. Because post-stroke outcome depends on balancing neuronal survival, stress granule biology, and reparative angiogenesis, RNASE1 emerges as a biologically compelling candidate with potential relevance to both acute injury modulation and later vascular remodeling.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170) 

Finally, WFDC2 provides a possible link to protease-driven vascular and inflammatory injury, which is another important component of post-stroke pathology. WFDC2 is potentially relevant to stroke because protease activity is a major determinant of post-stroke tissue injury, blood-brain barrier disruption, extracellular matrix degradation, and inflammatory remodeling. Broad-spectrum protease inhibitors can influence the balance between destructive proteolysis and controlled repair. In ischemic stroke, excessive protease activity contributes to vascular leakage, edema, leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhagic transformation, particularly during reperfusion. Although the present annotation is brief and does not specify the target proteases or provide stroke-focused evidence, the general function of WFDC2 suggests a plausible role in modulating protease-driven secondary injury. It therefore merits consideration as a candidate linked to vascular and inflammatory aspects of stroke pathology.
